claim: Respiration can induce motion and CO2 fluctuation during resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) scans, which will lead to non-neural artifacts in the rsfMRI signal.
source: Respiration can induce motion and CO2 fluctuation during resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) scans, which will lead to non-neural artifacts in the rsfMRI signal.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of fMRI research, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Respiration can directly drive neural activity change in the brain, and may thereby modulate the rsfMRI signal.
source: In the meantime, as a crucial physiologic process, respiration can directly drive neural activity change in the brain, and may thereby modulate the rsfMRI signal.
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the abstract, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Respiration is associated with neural activity changes, evidenced by a phase-locking relationship between slow respiration variations and the gamma-band power of the electrophysiological signal recorded in the anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Our data show that respiration is indeed associated with neural activity changes, evidenced by a phase-locking relationship between slow respiration variations and the gamma-band power of the electrophysiological signal recorded in the anterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing coherence between RVT and gamma-band power with zero phase lag (Figure 2D, E).

claim: Slow respiration variations are linked to a characteristic rsfMRI network, which is mediated by gamma-band neural activity.
source: Intriguingly, slow respiration variations are also linked to a characteristic rsfMRI network, which is mediated by gamma-band neural activity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that regressing out gamma power diminishes the respiration-related network (Figure 4D, E).

claim: The respiration-related brain network disappears when brain-wide neural activity is silenced at an isoelectrical state, while the respiration is maintained.
source: In addition, this respiration-related brain network disappears when brain-wide neural activity is silenced at an isoelectrical state, while the respiration is maintained, further confirming the necessary role of neural activity in this network.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing absence of the respiration-related network in the isoelectric state (Figure 5J).

claim: Resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI) measures spontaneous blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal.
source: Resting-state fMRI (rsfMRI), which measures spontaneous blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) signal, is a powerful tool for non-invasively investigating brain-wide functional connectivity (Biswal et al., 1995; Fox and Raichle, 2007; Smith et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The rsfMRI signal is susceptible to systemic physiological changes such as respiration and cardiac pulsations.
source: Due to its hemodynamic nature, the rsfMRI signal is susceptible to systemic physiological changes such as respiration and cardiac pulsations (Murphy et al., 2013; Liu, 2016; Caballero-Gaudes and Reynolds, 2017; Chen et al., 2020), and these effects are usually treated as non-neuronal artifacts in rsfMRI data.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Respiration is a major physiological process that drives fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and oxygenation.
source: Respiration is a major physiological process that drives fluctuations in cerebral blood flow and oxygenation (Liu, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Respiration can affect the BOLD signal with two types of effects resulting from slow respiration variations and fast cyclic changes, respectively.
source: Respiration can affect the BOLD signal (Thomason et al., 2005; Abbott et al., 2005; Birn et al., 2006) with two types of effects resulting from slow respiration variations and fast cyclic changes, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Slowly varying changes (typically below 0.15 Hz) in breathing rate and depth can be quantified as respiration volume per time (RVT).
source: Slowly varying changes (typically below 0.15 Hz) in breathing rate and depth, which can be quantified as respiration volume per time (RVT) (Birn et al., 2006), covary with arterial CO2 (Wise et al., 2004; Chang and Glover, 2009; Hoiland et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017) and affect the BOLD signal via vasodilatory effects and/or autonomic influences of the vessel tone (Duyn et al., 2020; Picchioni et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Slow respiration variations covary with arterial CO2 and affect the BOLD signal via vasodilatory effects and/or autonomic influences of the vessel tone.
source: Slowly varying changes (typically below 0.15 Hz) in breathing rate and depth, which can be quantified as respiration volume per time (RVT) (Birn et al., 2006), covary with arterial CO2 (Wise et al., 2004; Chang and Glover, 2009; Hoiland et al., 2016; Liu et al., 2017) and affect the BOLD signal via vasodilatory effects and/or autonomic influences of the vessel tone (Duyn et al., 2020; Picchioni et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Faster respiratory cycles, accompanied by chest and neck movement, can induce changes in the static magnetic field, which in turn lead to BOLD signal changes.
source: On the other hand, faster respiratory cycles (i.e., periodic inspiration and expiration), accompanied by the corresponding chest and neck movement, can induce changes in the static magnetic field, which in turn lead to BOLD signal changes (Glover et al., 2000; Raj et al., 2000; Windischberger et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Both slow and fast respiration effects can be effectively mitigated/removed by standard rsfMRI preprocessing methods.
source: Both effects can be effectively mitigated/removed by standard rsfMRI preprocessing methods (Birn et al., 2006; Glover et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Respiration can directly drive brain-wide neuronal oscillations not only in the olfactory bulb and piriform cortex but also in the medial prefrontal cortex, somatosensory cortex, and hippocampus.
source: First, respiration can directly drive brain-wide neuronal oscillations (Tort et al., 2018a; Kay et al., 2009) not only in the olfactory bulb (Adrian, 1942) and piriform cortex (Fontanini et al., 2003)—brain regions directly related to breathing—but also in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), somatosensory cortex, and hippocampus, and this effect has been consistently found across species (Ito et al., 2014; Yanovsky et al., 2014; Biskamp et al., 2017; Zelano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Respiration changes can be associated with arousal and/or emotion-related brain state changes, which covary with cortical activity.
source: In addition, respiration changes can be associated with arousal and/or emotion-related brain state changes, which covary with cortical activity (Yackle et al., 2017; Shea, 1996; Homma and Masaoka, 2008; Folschweiller and Sauer, 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Prominent coherence between the respiration signal and LFP is observed with the dominant peak at ~1.1 Hz.
source: Prominent coherence between the respiration signal and LFP is observed with the dominant peak at ~1.1 Hz (Figure 2B, C), in line with the respiration frequency in animals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The coherence between respiration signal and LFP at ~1.1 Hz is consistent with the finding of respiration-entrained LFP oscillations previously reported.
source: This result is consistent with the finding of respiration-entrained LFP oscillations previously reported (Tort et al., 2018a; Kay et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Gamma-band power displays significant coherence with the RVT at ~0.035 Hz with a zero phase lag.
source: Gamma-band power displays significant coherence with the RVT at ~0.035 Hz with a zero phase lag (Figure 2D, E, phase [mean ± ste] = −0.08 ± 0.5 pi, with the range of [−pi, pi]), suggesting a phase-locking relationship between the two measures.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: There is a phase-locking relationship between gamma-band power and RVT.
source: Gamma-band power displays significant coherence with the RVT at ~0.035 Hz with a zero phase lag (Figure 2D, E, phase [mean ± ste] = −0.08 ± 0.5 pi, with the range of [−pi, pi]), suggesting a phase-locking relationship between the two measures.
evidence: This is inferred from the zero phase lag observed in the data.

claim: No coherence is observed between RVT and delta-band, theta-band, alpha-band, or beta-band power.
source: In contrast, this coherence is not observed in any other frequency bands (Figure 2F–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F-I.

claim: The gamma power-derived rsfMRI correlation map is highly consistent with the ACC resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) seedmap.
source: Our data show that the gamma power-derived rsfMRI correlation map (Figure 3C) is highly consistent with the ACC resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) seedmap with the right ACC (i.e., the electrode implanted side) defined as the seed (Figure 3D), evidenced by a strong voxel-to-voxel spatial correlation between these two maps (Figure 3E, R = 0.775, p < 10−15).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing strong spatial correlation (R = 0.775, p < 10−15) between the two maps.

claim: The gamma-band LFP is tightly linked to the rsfMRI signal.
source: These data demonstrate that the gamma-band LFP is tightly linked to the rsfMRI signal.
evidence: This is inferred from the high spatial correlation between gamma power-derived correlation map and ACC RSFC seedmap.

claim: Slow respiration variations exhibit a characteristic correlation pattern with brain-wide rsfMRI signals, representing a respiration-related rsfMRI network.
source: Taken together, slow respiration variations exhibit a characteristic correlation pattern with brain-wide rsfMRI signals, representing a respiration-related rsfMRI network.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing voxel-wise correlations between RVT and rsfMRI signals (Figure 4B, C).

claim: The respiration-related rsfMRI network involves key brain regions controlling respiration such as the piriform cortex.
source: This analysis generates a respiration-related rsfMRI network (Figure 4B), involving key brain regions controlling respiration such as the piriform cortex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The respiration-related network includes regions involved in the rodent DMN such as the ACC, mPFC, orbital, retrosplenial, and primary somatosensory cortices, as well as the hippocampus.
source: In addition, this network includes regions involved in the rodent DMN such as the ACC, mPFC, orbital, retrosplenial, and primary somatosensory cortices, as well as the hippocampus (Lu et al., 2012; Figure 4C, one-sample t-test, p < 0.05, false discovery rate [FDR] corrected).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C with statistical significance (p < 0.05, FDR corrected).

claim: The resemblance of the respiration-related network and DMN agrees with the human literature that the physiological effects on rsfMRI data are colocalized with the DMN.
source: The resemblance of this respiration-related network and DMN well agrees with the human literature that the physiological effects on rsfMRI data are colocalized with the DMN (Birn et al., 2006).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Regressing out gamma power from RVT and rsfMRI signals diminishes the respiration-related network.
source: In this case, the respiration-related network is diminished (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: All brain regions involved in the respiration-related network exhibit reduced RVT–rsfMRI correlation after the gamma power is regressed out.
source: This result is confirmed by the contrast of the correlation maps before (Figure 4B) and after (Figure 4D) gamma power regression, with essentially all brain regions involved in the respiration-related network exhibiting reduced RVT–rsfMRI correlation after the gamma power is regressed out (Figure 4E, paired t-test, p < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E with statistical significance (p < 0.05, FDR corrected).

claim: The respiration-related rsfMRI network is mediated by gamma-band neural activity.
source: These results demonstrate that the respiration-related rsfMRI network is mediated by gamma-band neural activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that regressing out gamma power diminishes the respiration-related network.

claim: At the isoelectric state, the LFP amplitude and power are close to zero.
source: At the isoelectric state, the LFP amplitude and power are close to zero, in remarkable contrast to the electrophysiology data recorded before the drug infusion (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: rsfMRI data recorded at the isoelectric state exhibit a flat, noise-like power distribution, unlike the characteristic 1/f pattern during light sedation.
source: In addition, rsfMRI data recorded at the isoelectric state exhibit a flat, noise-like power distribution, unlike the characteristic 1/f pattern during light sedation (Figure 5I; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: There is no meaningful ACC RSFC in the ACC seedmap at the isoelectric state.
source: Furthermore, there is no meaningful ACC RSFC in the ACC seedmap at the isoelectric state (Figure 5H), which is distinct from the ACC seedmap during light sedation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The brain-wide ROI-based RSFC matrix reveals a global suppression of RSFC at the isoelectric state compared to light sedation.
source: The brain-wide ROI-based RSFC matrix also reveals a global suppression of RSFC at the isoelectric state (Figure 5K), compared to the RSFC matrix observed during light sedation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: Brain-wide neural activity is silenced in the isoelectric state.
source: These data collectively confirm that brain-wide neural activity is silenced in the isoelectric state.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple observations including near-zero LFP, flat BOLD power spectrum, and suppressed RSFC.

claim: There is no significant difference in the standard deviation of the respiration rate between the light sedation and isoelectric states.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in the SD of the respiration rate (Figure 5E, two-sample t-test, t = −1.0, p = 0.32) or the SD of RVT (Figure 5F, two-sample t-test, t = −0.87, p = 0.39) between the light sedation and isoelectric states, suggesting that the temporal variance of respiration is similar between the two states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical testing (t = −1.0, p = 0.32).

claim: There is no significant difference in the standard deviation of RVT between the light sedation and isoelectric states.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in the SD of the respiration rate (Figure 5E, two-sample t-test, t = −1.0, p = 0.32) or the SD of RVT (Figure 5F, two-sample t-test, t = −0.87, p = 0.39) between the light sedation and isoelectric states, suggesting that the temporal variance of respiration is similar between the two states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical testing (t = −0.87, p = 0.39).

claim: The temporal variance of respiration is similar between the light sedation and isoelectric states.
source: We did not observe any significant difference in the SD of the respiration rate (Figure 5E, two-sample t-test, t = −1.0, p = 0.32) or the SD of RVT (Figure 5F, two-sample t-test, t = −0.87, p = 0.39) between the light sedation and isoelectric states, suggesting that the temporal variance of respiration is similar between the two states.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of significant difference in SD of respiration rate and RVT.

claim: A characteristic 1/f pattern is observed in the RVT power during light sedation, but this pattern is not present at the isoelectric state.
source: Interestingly, we observed a characteristic 1/f pattern in the RVT power during light sedation, but this pattern was not present at the isoelectric state (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The respiration-related network observed during light sedation is absent when brain-wide neural activity is silenced.
source: The respiration-related network observed during light sedation is absent when brain-wide neural activity is silenced (Figure 5J), despite similar breathing patterns (Figure 5C–F) at both conditions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Neural activity plays a necessary role in the respiration-related rsfMRI network.
source: These data demonstrate that the neural activity plays a necessary role in the respiration-related rsfMRI network, corroborating the notion that the respiration-related rsfMR network we observed is mediated by neural activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of the respiration-related network when neural activity is silenced.

claim: No appreciable correlations are observed between RETROICOR and the rsfMRI signals across the brain in either the light sedation or isoelectric state.
source: Unlike the respiration-related neural network described above, we did not observe any appreciable correlations between RETROICOR and the rsfMRI signals across the brain in either the light sedation or isoelectric state (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact is distinct from the respiration-related neural network.
source: Our data show that the slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact is distinct from the respiration-related neural network.
evidence: This is inferred from differences in spatial patterns and response to preprocessing.

claim: The slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact is dominantly located around the ventricles and large veins.
source: First, the slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact is dominantly located around the ventricles and large veins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), whereas the respiration-related neural network is mostly located at the gray matter with a distinct spatial pattern (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The respiration-related neural network is mostly located at the gray matter with a distinct spatial pattern.
source: First, the slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact is dominantly located around the ventricles and large veins (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B), whereas the respiration-related neural network is mostly located at the gray matter with a distinct spatial pattern (Figure 4B, C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: The slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact can be reduced by regressing out the signals in the white matter and ventricles.
source: In addition, the slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact can be reduced by regressing out the signals in the white matter and ventricles (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C), but the respiration-induced neural network persists after the regression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The respiration-induced neural network persists after regressing out the signals in the white matter and ventricles.
source: In addition, the slow respiration-related rsfMRI artifact can be reduced by regressing out the signals in the white matter and ventricles (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C), but the respiration-induced neural network persists after the regression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The respiration-related neural network is not a non-neural physiological artifact but originates from neural activity.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the respiration-related neural network we observed is not a non-neural physiological artifact but originates from neural activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the distinct spatial patterns and differential responses to preprocessing between the neural network and artifacts.

claim: The respiration network is very likely linked to respiration-entrained brain-wide neural oscillations.
source: The respiration network is very likely linked to respiration-entrained brain-wide neural oscillations
evidence: This is inferred from consistency with previous literature on respiration-entrained neural oscillations.

claim: Respiration-induced neuronal oscillations have been consistently observed across multiple species including rats, mice, and humans.
source: Respiration-induced neuronal oscillations have been consistently observed across multiple species including rats, mice, and humans (Yanovsky et al., 2014; Zelano et al., 2016; Lockmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Respiration-induced neuronal oscillations are robust in various physiological and behavioral states including freely moving awake and immobile awake conditions, as well as anesthetized states.
source: This phenomenon also seems to be robust in various physiological and behavioral states including freely moving awake and immobile awake conditions, as well as anesthetized states (Fontanini et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2014; Zhong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies found that respiration specifically modulated the amplitude of gamma activity in the mPFC.
source: Intriguingly, previous studies found that respiration specifically modulated the amplitude of gamma activity in the mPFC (Zhong et al., 2017; Rojas-Líbano and Kay, 2008; Fontanini and Bower, 2005), consistent with our finding of band-specific coherence between the gamma power in the ACC and RVT.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, consistent with the current study's findings.

claim: Gamma power is generally believed to relate to the BOLD signal.
source: Notably, gamma power is generally believed to relate to the BOLD signal (Logothetis et al., 2001; Winder et al., 2017), which is also demonstrated in our study (Figure 3).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations and confirmed by data in the current study.

claim: Respiration-generated neuronal oscillations are phase locked to the breath rhythm across distributed brain regions including the olfactory bulb, primary piriform cortex, hippocampus, and somatosensory barrel cortex.
source: In addition to the mPFC, previous work has shown that respiration-generated neuronal oscillations are phase locked to the breath rhythm across distributed brain regions including the olfactory bulb, primary piriform cortex, hippocampus, and somatosensory barrel cortex (Fontanini et al., 2003; Ito et al., 2014; Yanovsky et al., 2014; Biskamp et al., 2017; Herrero et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The brain regions showing respiration-generated neuronal oscillations are highly consistent with brain regions in the respiration network observed in the current study.
source: Those regions are highly consistent with brain regions in the respiration network we observed.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison between the current study's findings and previous literature.

claim: The piriform cortex is anatomically connected to the mPFC, ACC, and orbital cortex.
source: Furthermore, the piriform cortex is anatomically connected to the mPFC, ACC, and orbital cortex, all of which are parts of the respiration network in our study (Schmahmann, 2009; Illig, 2005; García-Cabezas and Barbas, 2014; Carmichael et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The spatial pattern of the respiration network agrees with brain regions exhibiting neural oscillation changes driven by respiration.
source: Taken together, the spatial pattern of the respiration network reported here well agrees with brain regions exhibiting neural oscillation changes driven by respiration.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with previous literature on respiration-driven neural oscillations.

claim: Respiration-induced neuronal oscillations do not result from the movement of the muscle or electrode.
source: Previous work also demonstrates that respiration-induced neuronal oscillations do not result from the movement of the muscle or electrode.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work.

claim: The oscillations are different in the laminar amplitude along the hippocampus, with the maximal amplitude in the dentate gyrus (DG).
source: For instance, the oscillations are different in the laminar amplitude along the hippocampus, with the maximal amplitude in the dentate gyrus (DG) (Yanovsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The finding of maximal oscillation amplitude in the DG agrees with the current study's data showing more prominent involvement of the DG than other parts of the hippocampus in the respiration network.
source: This finding well agrees with our data, displaying more prominent involvement of the DG than other parts of the hippocampus in the respiration network.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison between the current study's findings and previous literature.

claim: Only the gamma-band power, not other LFP bands, is coherent with slow variations of respiration.
source: In addition, our data show that only the gamma-band power, not other LFP bands, is coherent with slow variations of respiration, whereas the movement of electrode or muscle would lead to increased coherence across multiple frequency bands.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Movement of electrode or muscle would lead to increased coherence across multiple frequency bands.
source: In addition, our data show that only the gamma-band power, not other LFP bands, is coherent with slow variations of respiration, whereas the movement of electrode or muscle would lead to increased coherence across multiple frequency bands.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about artifacts from electrode or muscle movement.

claim: Regressing out the respirational signal does not abolish the RSFC measured by rsfMRI data.
source: Notably, regressing out the respirational signal does not abolish the RSFC measured by rsfMRI data, suggesting that the respiration does not account for all the effects of the RSFC measured.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that RSFC patterns remain after RVT regression.

claim: RVT regression reduced ACC RSFC particularly in brain regions involved in the respiration network, but the major RSFC pattern remains consistent.
source: Although RVT regression reduced ACC RSFC particularly in brain regions involved in the respiration network as expected, the major RSFC pattern remains consistent, indicating that a dominant component of RSFC is not ascribed by the respiration effect.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: A dominant component of RSFC is not ascribed by the respiration effect.
source: Although RVT regression reduced ACC RSFC particularly in brain regions involved in the respiration network as expected, the major RSFC pattern remains consistent, indicating that a dominant component of RSFC is not ascribed by the respiration effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of major RSFC patterns after RVT regression.

claim: The neural contribution to the respiration-related brain network may be mediated by arousal changes, which is associated with both neural excitability and respiration.
source: It is possible that the neural contribution to the respiration-related brain network is mediated by arousal changes, which is associated with both neural excitability and respiration (Yackle et al., 2017; Shea, 1996; Fan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation based on cited literature.

claim: The cerebral blood flow can be regulated by the innervation from the basal forebrain and locus coeruleus, and both regions are directly related to arousal changes.
source: The cerebral blood flow can be regulated by the innervation from the basal forebrain and locus coeruleus, and both regions are directly related to arousal changes (Yackle et al., 2017; Lecrux and Hamel, 2016; Melnychuk et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies in humans demonstrated correlations among the fMRI signal, low-frequency fluctuations of respiration, and EEG alpha power.
source: Previous studies in humans demonstrated correlations among the fMRI signal, low-frequency fluctuations of respiration, and EEG alpha power (Yuan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The fMRI–respiration correlate was stronger at the eye-closing resting state with a greater arousal-level change than the eye-open state.
source: The fMRI–respiration correlate was stronger at the eye-closing resting state with a greater arousal-level change than the eye-open state.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The arousal level does not play a dominant role in the current study's results.
source: However, we do not believe the arousal level plays a dominant role in our results, given that our study was performed in anesthetized animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design using anesthetized animals.

claim: No coherence was observed between alpha-band power and the slow variations of respiration in the current study.
source: Accordingly, we did not observe any coherence between alpha-band power and the slow variations of respiration, suggesting the respiration-related fMRI network we observed might be attributed to a different mechanism than arousal.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The respiration-related fMRI network observed in the current study might be attributed to a different mechanism than arousal.
source: Accordingly, we did not observe any coherence between alpha-band power and the slow variations of respiration, suggesting the respiration-related fMRI network we observed might be attributed to a different mechanism than arousal.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of coherence between alpha-band power and respiration.

claim: The findings in the present study echo the results reported in human studies.
source: The findings in the present study to a large extent echo the results reported in human studies.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with human literature.

claim: Previous research demonstrated bidirectional interplay between respiration and neural activity in humans.
source: Previous research demonstrated bidirectional interplay between respiration and neural activity in humans.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Neural activity in brainstem regions such as the preBötzinger complex directly controls the respiration.
source: Neural activity in brainstem regions such as the preBötzinger complex directly controls the respiration (Baertsch et al., 2021; Smith et al., 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Respiration-induced LFP oscillations were observed in multiple human brain regions such as the piriform cortex and hippocampus.
source: In addition, respiration-induced LFP oscillations were observed in multiple human brain regions such as the piriform cortex and hippocampus (Zelano et al., 2016; Herrero et al., 2018), consistent with our data.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations, consistent with the current study.

claim: Voluntary hyperpnea was related to the neural activity of various brain regions including the primary sensory and motor cortices, supplementary motor area, caudate nucleus, and globus pallidum.
source: McKay et al. also found that voluntary hyperpnea was related to the neural activity of various brain regions including the primary sensory and motor cortices, supplementary motor area, caudate nucleus, and globus pallidum, which largely agree with the respiration-related brain network we identified in rats (McKay et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation, consistent with the current study.

claim: Respiration-mediated neural activity was found to modulate brain function.
source: Importantly, respiration-mediated neural activity was found to modulate brain function.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous research.

claim: Respiration modulates visual perceptual sensitivity, mediated by alpha power.
source: For example, respiration is shown to modulate visual perceptual sensitivity, mediated by alpha power (Kluger et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Respiration is a key component in mindfulness meditation, which has been repeatedly shown to have modulatory effects on brain function.
source: Respiration is also the key component in mindfulness meditation, which has been repeatedly shown to have modulatory effects on brain function (Doll et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Stimulation of the pedunculopontine region (PPNr) improved upper airway function in Parkinson's patients.
source: Hyam et al. stimulated the pedunculopontine region (PPNr) and observed improvement in upper airway function in Parkinson's patients (Hyam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Loss of neurons in the preBötzinger complex causes sleep-disordered breathing.
source: Loss of neurons in the preBötzinger complex was found to cause sleep-disordered breathing (McKay et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The respiration-related brain network might be conserved across species and represent a general phenomenon in the mammalian brain.
source: Taken together, those findings indicate that the respiration-related brain network might be conserved across species and represent a general phenomenon in the mammalian brain, and this brain network might play an important role in normal and diseased brain function.
evidence: This is inferred from consistency of findings across species.

claim: The respiration-related brain network might play an important role in normal and diseased brain function.
source: Taken together, those findings indicate that the respiration-related brain network might be conserved across species and represent a general phenomenon in the mammalian brain, and this brain network might play an important role in normal and diseased brain function.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: Anesthesia might be a potential confounder as it may affect the respiration, as well as respiration-induced neural and vascular activities.
source: However, it has to be recognized that anesthesia might be a potential confounder by itself, as it may affect the respiration, as well as respiration-induced neural and vascular activities.
evidence: This is speculation about potential limitations of the study.

claim: Anesthetics can reduce the respiration rate and affect LFP by increasing the low-frequency power and decreasing the high-frequency power.
source: For instance, anesthetics can reduce the respiration rate and affect LFP by increasing the low-frequency power and decreasing the high-frequency power (Purdon et al., 2013; You et al., 2021; Bastos et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Isoflurane is a vasodilator, which can attenuate the BOLD signal.
source: Isoflurane is a vasodilator, which can attenuate the BOLD signal (Schwinn et al., 1990), whereas the dexmedetomidine is a vasoconstrictor, which can counteract the vasodilatory effect from isoflurane (Talke and Anderson, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.
